Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australia news Analysis Amid claims of ‘mass migration’, Labor hopes a measured approach will take the hot air out of the debate Patrick Commins The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix? Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Tony Burke has promised to make Labor’s existing migration policy work better rather than announcing a dramatic cut in numbers, arguing that populist promises to slash net overseas migration will “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”. The home affairs minister’s message was immediately endorsed by employer groups, who over recent days have made it clear that steps to arbitrarily slash migrant numbers would compound already severe skills shortages and hurt businesses, especially those in the regions. “We need immigration. We just need to make sure that it is targeted for the needs of Australia in numbers and across the different categories that work for our economy,” Burke said in his long-awaited address to the National Press Club on Thursday. “We talk about the need for extra housing. It’s pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved. In both Sydney and Melbourne, close to two-thirds of the plasterers we have were born overseas.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Bran Black, the chief executive of the Business Council in Australia, welcomed the government’s efforts to “restore integrity to the migration system”, even as he argued against new rules that would limit the length of stay for most backpackers. “The starting point for migration policy should not be a number to cut to, but what our economy genuinely needs,” Black said. “Almost one in three occupations in this country are short of workers right now. That translates to not enough workers building homes, caring for us in hospitals and aged care homes, delivering infrastructure and powering the energy transition. That is the challenge that any migration policy should be looking to solve.” Labor has taken a long time to come up with its policy prescription to fix the country’s migration settings which, after the post-pandemic surge in new arrivals, have become a source of growing popular discontent. Spurious claims of “mass migration” have fanned the flames of this discontent, but few would argue that our system is working well and in the best interests of the country – or in the best interests of a ballooning number of people trapped in a kind of temporary visa limbo that has strained public infrastructure and patience. Backpacker ballot and detention centre for visa overstayers: what we know about Australia’s new migration plan Read more Alan Gamlen, the director of the ANU’s migration hub, said Burke appeared to have announced the right mix of measures that would give the government the capacity to regulate an out-of-control temporary visa system without damaging the economy. “They don’t seem to have fallen into the trap of chasing a net migration number,” Gamlen said. “Burke made it pretty clear, and in a convincing way, that this is the result of a well-considered process that has been going on for a while and which addresses long-term structural issues, rather than just a kneejerk response to One Nation.” One Nation has committed to lowering net overseas migration to 130,000 a year, and the Coalition somewhere between 150,000 and 170,000. In comparison, Burke stuck to the government’s forecast of 225,000 people by 2027-28. He did, however, acknowledge that there was now a public expectation that the government would pull the levers necessary to get there. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Net overseas migration has been viewed as a budget forecast. Last couple of years, people have talked about it as a budget target,” he said. “That is a very different way of looking at it. But given that we have the challenges we have with housing in Australia at the moment, I do think we need to be able to have these additional tools to make sure that what is published and forecast is reached.” With business groups already suffering from skills shortages even at a time of high immigration, the home affairs minister articulated why he believed the government can win the political argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom. “The lower [Nom] levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy,” he said. Burke pointed out that denying skilled foreign workers the opportunity to bring in family members – as proposed by One Nation – would not free up more visas for more workers. Instead, that approach would slash the number of foreign doctors, tradies, nurses and aged care workers willing to come to our country. “The proportion of doctors who come to Australia with family attached to their application? 50%. How many construction workers come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many nurses and aged care workers come with family attached to their application? Two-thirds.” Whether Burke and the Albanese government can convince the public its measured approach is enough is an open question. “Let’s see if this lets out some of the hot air in the migration debate,” Gamlen said. WASHINGTON -- Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad. “I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously." Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory. The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats,” saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful.” He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO. Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance. “Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said. Latvian Defense Minister: ‘Russia Will Use Any Means To Threaten Us’ by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:50 0:00 Escalation Risks? The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use. Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences. SEE ALSO: Putin Rattles The Nuclear Saber Again. Bluster? Probably, Experts Say. He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.” Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective. But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue. She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited. “The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said. Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously. Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia. Kaliningrad WEBMAP Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability. She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use. Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad. Hybrid Attacks For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity -- hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponization of migration. He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure. “We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing. SEE ALSO: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine. “Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously. He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus -- which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilize its neighbors -- and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies. SEE ALSO: Baltic States Arm For Russian Threat As Leaked Letter Shows Growing Fears Latvia is also strengthening defenses against drones. Melnis said the country had deployed interceptor systems and additional radar along its borders with Russia and Belarus, drawing heavily on lessons from Ukraine. NATO fighter aircraft provide another layer, while Latvia is procuring medium- and short-range air defense systems. Melnis said Russian drone incursions could become a growing feature of the Baltic security environment, citing recent incidents involving Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Latvia, he said, is preparing for more such incidents. US Role In European Defense Melnis was in Washington to deepen defense cooperation with the US, including discussions involving the Michigan National Guard, procurement programs, and capability development. He said he remains confident that the US will maintain a military presence in Europe despite adjustments to deployments in individual countries. US forces, he said, remain in Latvia, and Washington continues to recognize the strategic importance of the region. At the same time, Melnis said European allies must assume a greater share of the burden for their own defense. He credited US President Donald Trump with pushing NATO members to increase defense spending, saying Latvia is committed by law to spending at least 5 percent of gross domestic product annually on security beginning next year . NATO members agreed at their 2025 summit in The Hague to spend 5 percent of GDP annually on defense and defense-related priorities by 2035, up from the alliance’s previous 2-percent benchmark. Latvia has moved faster, with its parliament requiring national defense spending of at least 5 percent of projected GDP from 2027. But Melnis said greater European responsibility would go hand in hand with continued US support. “The United States will provide. They will be there. They will fight with us if needed,” Melnis said, while stressing that Europe must do more.
